document.abstract: This paper describes a new high-quality deinterlacing algorithm applying motion estimation and compensation techniques. First, a comparison between two recently introduced deinterlacing concepts will be presented. One method is based on a generalized sampling theorem and the other uses time recursion. The new algorithm aims at combining the benefits of both.

authors.bio: Erwin Bellers received a B.Sc. degree from the Technische Hogeschool Enschede in 1987 and an M.Sc. degree (with destinction) from the University of Twente in 1993. In December 1993, he joined Philips Research Laboratories in Eindhoven as a research scientist in the Television Systems Group. He worked on several video processing projects, with major interest in video enhancement algorithms. At present Bellers contributes to the area of motion estimation, motion compensation, and deinterlacing and scan rate conversion.

authors.bio: Gerard de Haan received B.Sc., M.Sc., and Ph.D. degrees from Delft University of Technology in 1977, 1979, and 1992, respectively. In 1979 he joined the Philips Research Laboratories in Eindhoven, where he led several research projects in the area of image processing and participated in a number of European projects. He has coached students from various universities, and since 1988 teaches at the Philips Centre for Technical Training. In 1991–1992, he was a visiting researcher in the Information Theory Group of Delft University. At present, he is a senior scientist in the Television Systems Group of Philips Research and has a particular interest in algorithms for motion estimation, scan rate conversion, and image enhancement. His work in these areas has resulted in about 35 patents and patent applica- tions, and the 1995 ICCE Outstanding Paper Award. He was responsible for the algorithmic design of the 100-Hz TV with “Natural Motion,” for which Philips received the European Innovation Award of the Year for 1995–1996 from the European Imaging and Sound Association.
